entries.cause: Agrotis ipsilon (black or greasy cutworm) and related Agrotis species; moth larvae
symptoms: Caterpillars hide in soil during the day and feed at night.
Older caterpillars cut young plant stems at ground level.
Young caterpillars first feed on the leaf surface.
Full-grown caterpillar is dirty black or dark brown with a greasy look.
Tubers can also be eaten into.
entries.look_alikes: Armyworms feed on leaves in groups and do not cut seedlings at the base; white grubs eat roots underground.
cultural_actions: Flood the field and hand-pick caterpillars in the morning or evening.
Plough in summer to expose caterpillars and pupae to birds.
Use light traps and pheromone traps to watch for moths.
entries.when_to_act: Spray only when scouting shows cut seedlings or caterpillars; check the local threshold with your KVK.

entries.cause: Nilaparvata lugens (brown planthopper) and Sogatella furcifera (white-backed planthopper); sap-sucking insects of rice
symptoms: Small insects sit at the base of rice plants and suck sap.
Brown planthopper adults are yellowish to dark brown; white-backed has a white band on the back.
Plants yellow, turn brown and dry in round or irregular patches called hopper burn.
Affected patches can lodge and look scorched.
Sooty mould and honeydew may show at the plant base.
entries.look_alikes: Stem borer deadhearts are single dead shoots, not dried patches with insects at the base.
cultural_actions: Drain the field briefly during early attack.
Give nitrogen in split doses and avoid too much nitrogen.
Plant together within a short window across the area.
Leave rogue spacing lanes through the field.
Protect spiders, mirid bugs and other natural enemies.
Use light traps at night and yellow pan traps by day.

treatment_options.note: Natural enemy listed by TNAU; protect it, do not spray it out

entries.when_to_act: TNAU gives a hopper-per-tiller threshold that is lower when spiders are absent; check the local threshold with your KVK.

entries.cause: Scirpophaga incertulas (yellow stem borer); larvae bore inside rice stems
symptoms: Female moth is bright yellowish brown with a black spot on the forewing.
Larva is pale yellow with a dark brown head and bores into the stem.
Early attack: central shoot dries, called dead heart; it pulls out easily.
Later attack: panicle dries and grains are chaffy, called white ear.
Brown egg masses sit near the leaf tip.
entries.look_alikes: Planthopper hopper burn comes in dried patches with insects at the base; gall midge makes a silver onion-leaf tube.
cultural_actions: Clip seedling tips before transplanting to remove egg masses.
Scout the field regularly.
Disturb or destroy stubble after harvest.
Use light traps and pheromone traps to watch moths.
Release the egg parasitoid Trichogramma japonicum as advised by the source.
Choose resistant varieties recommended for your area.

treatment_options.active_ingredient: Neem seed kernel extract or azadirachtin

entries.when_to_act: TNAU gives thresholds as egg masses, dead hearts and white ears; check the local threshold with your KVK.

ask_back.question: Do the central shoots dry and pull out easily, with a bored stem inside?
Is there a silver, onion-like tube instead of a dead shoot?

entries.cause: Cnaphalocrocis medinalis (rice leaf folder moth); larvae fold rice leaves
symptoms: Caterpillars fold a leaf lengthwise and live inside it.
They scrape the green tissue from inside the fold.
Damaged leaves turn white and dry.
In severe attack the whole field looks scorched.
entries.look_alikes: Planthopper burn dries whole patches from the base; folded leaves with a caterpillar inside point to leaf folder.
cultural_actions: Avoid too much nitrogen fertiliser.
Keep field bunds clean.
Release Trichogramma chilonis egg parasitoids as the source advises.
Clip affected leaves where practical, as TNAU lists.
Choose resistant varieties recommended for your area.

treatment_options.active_ingredient: Neem seed kernel extract or azadirachtin

entries.when_to_act: TNAU gives a leaf-damage threshold that is different for early growth and the flag leaf stage; check the local threshold with your KVK.

ask_back.question: Are leaves folded lengthwise with a caterpillar inside and white scraped streaks?

entries.cause: Orseolia oryzae (Asian rice gall midge); a small fly whose maggots attack the rice shoot
symptoms: Adult is a small yellowish-brown or orange fly, like a mosquito.
Tiny maggots enter the growing bud at the shoot base.
The shoot turns into a hollow tube like an onion leaf, called silver shoot.
Infested tillers give no panicle, so yield falls.
entries.look_alikes: Stem borer deadheart is a dried shoot; gall midge gives a green-silver onion-leaf tube.
cultural_actions: Plough the field soon after harvest.
Remove alternate host plants and grasses.
Plant early, as TNAU advises.
Apply potash in balance.
Use infrared light traps to monitor adult flies.
Grow resistant varieties listed for your area.

treatment_options.note: Natural enemy listed by TNAU; follow local extension advice

entries.when_to_act: TNAU gives a silver-shoot percentage threshold; check the local threshold with your KVK.

ask_back.question: Do you see hollow silver-white onion-leaf tubes in place of tillers?

entries.cause: Mythimna separata and Spodoptera mauritia (swarming caterpillar); fall armyworm Spodoptera frugiperda also attacks maize
symptoms: Caterpillars feed in groups and march from field to field.
They cut seedlings in large numbers.
Heavily eaten fields look like cattle have grazed them.
On rice and maize they eat leaf edges and can cut panicles.
Young caterpillars are light green; older ones turn brownish with dark marks.
entries.look_alikes: Cutworms act alone and cut single stems at ground level; armyworms come in groups and eat leaves too.
cultural_actions: Flood nurseries so caterpillars are exposed to birds.
Let ducks and birds feed on the caterpillars.
Dig trenches filled with ash around the field as a barrier.
Bury stubble after harvest and keep fields weed-free.
Use pheromone traps and natural enemies like Telenomus remus for fall armyworm in maize.

entries.cause: Wireworms are the soil-living larvae of click beetles (Elateridae)
symptoms: Larvae are tan to black, smooth, shiny and segmented.
They bore into seeds as they germinate.
They feed on roots, crowns and tubers.
Affected plants wilt; potato tubers get tunnelled.
entries.look_alikes: White grubs are fat and C-shaped; wireworms are thin, hard and shiny.
cultural_actions: Avoid planting susceptible crops where weedy pasture or grass was recently grown.
Remove dead plants promptly.
Plough several times in late spring and early summer.
Flood or dry the soil as the source describes, where practical.
Scout with grain bait traps buried in the soil.
entries.when_to_act: Source ties treatment to bait-trap counts; check the local threshold with your KVK.

entries.cause: Gryllotalpa orientalis (mole cricket); a burrowing soil insect
symptoms: Insect is brownish and plump with short antennae.
Front legs are wide and toothed for digging.
Seedlings are cut at the base.
Plants are lost, leaving gaps in the stand.
Roots are damaged and seedlings die.
entries.look_alikes: Cutworms are caterpillars that cut stems at night; mole crickets are digging insects with strong front legs.
cultural_actions: Keep standing water, which helps remove eggs on the soil.
Shave and plaster bunds with fresh wet soil to remove eggs.
Level the field for better water control.
Avoid raised nurseries.
Poisoned rice bran baits along bunds are mentioned by TNAU; ask your KVK which product.
entries.when_to_act: Source gives no threshold; check the local threshold with your KVK.
